nameStory: The common name "Soft Polypore" comes from its notably spongy, soft texture that feels almost like foam rubber when fresh. Unlike many bracket fungi that become rock-hard with age, this species maintains its cushiony feel, making it instantly recognizable by touch alone.
description: The Soft Polypore is a bracket fungus that grows like a shelf or fan from dead hardwood trees. It forms whitish to pale yellow semicircular brackets that can reach 4-8 inches across and feel remarkably soft and spongy to the touch. The underside is covered with tiny pores instead of gills, and the whole fungus has a clean, fresh appearance when young that gradually becomes more weathered and grayish with age.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels distinctly soft and spongy like a kitchen sponge or foam padding - this is the key identifying feature that sets it apart from other bracket fungi

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Semicircular shelf-like brackets that are white to pale yellow when fresh, becoming grayish with age, often with faint concentric zones

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Underside has white to cream-colored tiny round pores that may bruise slightly yellow when pressed, about 3-4 pores per millimeter

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Fresh specimens have a pleasant, mild mushroomy smell with no unpleasant odors

idTips.label: Attachment
idTips.description: Grows directly from wood without a stem, often in overlapping clusters that can be gently peeled away from the tree

habitat: Found on dead hardwood trees throughout New England's forests, particularly favoring oak, maple, and beech. Look for it in mixed deciduous and mixed hardwood-softwood forests from sea level to mid-elevations. It's commonly spotted along hiking trails where dead wood is abundant.

seasonality.spring: Fresh new brackets begin appearing on recently dead wood, displaying their characteristic bright white color and maximum sponginess.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with the most abundant fruiting bodies. Fresh specimens are at their softest and most identifiable during humid periods.
seasonality.fall: Mature brackets become more weathered and grayish but remain soft to touch. New growth may appear after autumn rains.
seasonality.winter: Old brackets persist on trees but become harder and less distinctive, though they rarely become as rigid as other polypores.

funFact: This fungus is so soft that mycologists sometimes use it as a natural field cushion when sitting to examine other specimens - it's literally nature's foam padding that grows on trees!
confusionNotes: Most often confused with other white bracket fungi like Trametes species, but the spongy texture is the instant giveaway - if you can compress it like a sponge, it's likely the Soft Polypore. Remember: "Soft to touch, Soft Polypore!"
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "polypore," this species was recently moved from the traditional polypore family into its own family (Cerrenaceae) based on DNA studies. This reflects ongoing changes in fungal classification as genetic analysis reveals evolutionary relationships.
compareHints: This is the only species in its genus found in New England, making identification easier once you know the key features. It differs from similar-looking bracket fungi in the Trametes genus by its distinctly softer texture and tendency to retain sponginess even when older. While Trametes species become tough and woody, Irpiciporus mollis stays pleasantly squeezable.
